decision: Memoize the compositor surface so the window plane's re-renders stop at it
why: This is the cause of every compositor effect flashing during a drag. The surface re-rendered on every store change, each render re-attached the canvas ref, and useConfigureContext disconnects and constructs a new ResizeObserver for each attach. A newly observed element always gets one callback, and that callback writes canvas.width, which resets the canvas and drops its WebGPU swap chain. The result is a blank frame with no error and correct data. @typegpu/react documents that per-frame values go through useFrame and .write() and never through a React render; the surface already reads the store with state$.peek() inside useFrame, so it needs no render of its own
evidence: Wrapped ResizeObserver and the canvas width setter on the live page. Before: a 30-frame drag constructed 60 observers, fired 29 callbacks and wrote canvas.width 29 times. After: 0, 0 and 0, with the backing size still 2300x1346
result: VERIFIED: owner confirmed the flashing is gone on the earlier workaround, and this root-cause fix reproduces that with the library's own autoResize left on. No upstream deficit; the earlier claim of one was wrong

decision: Rewrite backend/surface.tsx from scratch on the documented @typegpu/react and TypeGPU patterns: pipelines in useMemo, one useFrame, no useEffect, no useState, no readiness gate, no destroy hooks, and per-draw bare submissions via pipeline.withColorAttachment(target()).draw(n) with the first claim clearing and later claims loading
why: The owner required the file reworked from first principles. The old file mutated a ref during render, drove pass construction through useState so a teardown left a frame with zero passes, hand-rolled a dirty flag over the store's own reactivity, gated drawing behind Promise.allSettled and a cancelled flag, and hand-rolled a shared command encoder. TypeGPU's pipelines page documents loadOp clear then load for several pipelines on one canvas and states pipelines compile lazily on first draw, so the readiness gate had no basis
evidence: docs.swmansion.com/TypeGPU/apis/pipelines and the @typegpu/react README; renderPipeline.d.ts withColorAttachment; framework, playground, and Polkadot all type-check with zero errors; all three API gates pass
result: VERIFIED structurally by type-check and gates. The rewrite alone did NOT fix the flashing; the canvas reset above did

decision: Drive the contact shadow from each window's height in the stack: shadow lift, spread and faintness all scale with the normalized z already carried in WindowInstance.state.w, and each window casts its own shadow with the nearest winning instead of one union shaded once
why: The owner states the canvas is a world with depth and everything on it is diegetic. Depth is already uploaded per window as state.w, 0 at the back and 1 at the front, and no pass read it: radiance, focus field and contact shadow all treated every window as coplanar. The shadow offset every window by the same 6 pixels with the same softness, which is the CSS drop-shadow idiom rather than a depth cue

decision: Revise the scene-model spine to revision 2: split intent from state. The store says what the world should become; a GPU-resident world holds what it is and moves toward the intent by dt in one compute step before any pass draws. Window height becomes a world coordinate. Delete rather than tune the radiance pass, WindowInstance.state.w and InfiniteCanvasScenePass.frameloop
why: The owner states the canvas is a world with depth where everything is diegetic, and reports light changing instantly on focus. Revision 1 declared the scene model a pure derivation from state, which is the architecture the compositor already has. A pure projection of the current state has no previous value to move from, so continuity is unreachable in it; and its windows are rects with a stacking index, so depth is nominal. Radiance cascades solves a 2D field whose sdf and color hooks take a flat uv, so height cannot reach the lighting through its API
evidence: apps/compositor-poc/src/spine/scene-model-spine.tsx revision 2; surface.tsx rebuilds every frame from store.state$.peek(); instances.ts writes tint.w from a boolean so emission is a step function; the runner's own getCascadeDim and 2D uv hooks in node_modules/@typegpu/radiance-cascades
result: NOT VERIFIED: this is a spine revision, not production code. It supersedes revision 1 and needs review before any production write follows it. The lighting technique for a world with depth is deliberately left open as backlog item 7

decision: Build the world in production: compositor/backend/world.ts holds a GPU-resident body per window and one compute step moves it toward the document by dt before any pass draws. The surface uploads targets to a separate buffer and binds the instances accessor to the body buffer, so every pass reads the settled world with no pass edited

decision: Move the minimap window ladder off the ink scale and into the surface neutrals
why: The design system has two token families: neutral surfaces from L 0 through L 0.32, and warm ink from L 0.55 through L 0.96. Ink is glyph lightness. All three minimap window states filled with ink tokens, so the active window painted a solid block at L 0.72 — the brightest neutral anywhere in the product, on a ground the roadmap pins at L 0 with a surface scale that tops out near L 0.19. A prior pass had already caught half of this, moving active from --ink (0.96) to --ink-muted (0.72), and left a comment claiming the ladder had "three steps, none of them near white". That claim was still wrong by roughly a factor of three, because the fix stayed inside the wrong family instead of leaving it
evidence: apps/polkadot/src/hud/minimap.tsx: active --line-strong (0.32), selected --line (0.252), idle --surface-hover (0.19), groups --surface-raised (0.159) so a group still reads under the windows drawn over it. The framework owns only getInfiniteCanvasMinimapLayout, which returns geometry and no colour, so this is a product decision sitting in the right package and needs no framework change
result: VERIFIED in the running app at localhost:3001 by measuring the rendered rect, not by eye: computed fill reads oklch(0.32 0 0) where it read oklch(0.72 0.012 85) before. First reading of the same element returned the old value because the rect carries a 100ms fill transition and the sample landed mid-transition; the settled value is the one recorded. NOT VERIFIED: the idle and selected steps, which need a second window and a selection to exercise, and whether the three steps separate well enough at a 4px block is a look judgement only the owner can make

decision: Give the framework a real strip packer, and collapse the third and second copies of the rect union
why: The framework had no packer. Reading the five modules that decide where a window goes showed four classes and one hole: group-layout.ts partitions one bounded rect by a weight tree, so area is conserved and overlap is impossible by construction; window-arrange.ts is relational, moving rects that already exist; window-placement.ts is an online search for one new window, and by its own code path returns the least-bad overlapping rect when nothing clear is within its 169-candidate ring. Nothing took a set of windows and returned an arrangement. The right frame is strip packing rather than bin packing, because a canvas is fixed in width and unbounded in height, so the goal is to minimise height rather than a count of fixed bins. Found in passing and fixed here because it sat directly in the path: three private copies of the same rect union existed, geometry.ts unionRects with five callers plus a public export, and duplicates in window-arrange.ts and recipes.ts. The same pattern was already consolidated once for rectsEqual in 8742a6c
evidence: New packages/infinite-canvas/src/window-packing.ts holds getInfiniteCanvasPackedRects, First-Fit Decreasing Height from Coffman, Garey, Johnson and Tarjan 1980, which holds within 1.7 times the optimal height plus one level. It follows the house layout contract that window-arrange.ts already set, rects in and rects out, same length and order, sizes never changed, so it needed no adapter at the call site. Equal heights keep the caller's order, so tidying same-sized windows is deterministic. commands.ts gains window.pack routed through a new getArrangedRects, which replaces the nested ternary that had been duplicated in both the executor and the availability predicate, so a command can no longer be offered and then do nothing. window-arrange.ts and recipes.ts now call unionRects and their copies are deleted. New apps/playground/src/routes/packing.tsx shows it on 24 windows with a live occupancy readout
result: VERIFIED live at localhost:3300/packing by clicking the real button on the real command path, not by reading. Overlapping pairs went from 8 to 0 and occupancy from 86 to 92 per cent on 24 windows. The rows are the algorithm's own signature and cannot happen by accident: four rows, six windows each, every row sharing an exact top edge, and row heights strictly descending at 180, 150, 120 and 90 screen pixels. An earlier run of the same page proved nothing, because the stress generator makes windows of one height and the input already had zero overlaps, so the route now varies heights to exercise the sort. 817 tests pass across 103 files, unchanged in count, which is the evidence that deleting the two union copies preserved behaviour. Both affected packages check clean. NOT VERIFIED: whether FFDH beats Best-Fit skyline on occupancy here, which is unmeasured, and the online case, since window-placement.ts is untouched and still owns single-window placement

decision: Pack into the visible region rather than the width the windows already span, and give Polkadot the verb
why: Running the new command in Polkadot found an ergonomic defect that reading would not have: on a vertical stack of five windows it only tightened the column, 1296 down to 1264, because the strip width defaulted to the width the rects already covered and that can never widen anything. The user intent behind a pack button on a tall column is a compact block, not a slightly shorter column. The bound already has an owner: window-placement.ts uses getInfiniteCanvasContentWorldRect for where a new window may go, so packing uses the same rect rather than inventing a second notion of usable space. The pure function keeps its own bounds-width default, since a packer with no state should not invent a viewport
evidence: commands.ts: getArrangedRects now takes state and a new getPackingStripWidth supplies the visible content width, guarded by isUsableViewport so a headless or zero-sized viewport falls back to the packer's own default instead of a zero-width strip that would put every window on its own row. apps/polkadot/src/hud/canvas-hud.tsx gains one Verb in the selection rail beside align and distribute, disabled below two selected, passing a 16px gap because the packer itself leaves none and a workbench wants the windows to breathe
result: VERIFIED live in the playground at a real 676px viewport: the packed block changed from 2034 by 1116 to 616 by 3416, which is the proof the strip now comes from the viewport and not the bounds, with 24 windows in 12 rows of 2, occupancy 92 per cent and zero overlapping pairs. 817 tests pass across 103 files and both packages check clean. NOT VERIFIED in Polkadot: the button is present in the rail and executes, confirmed by reading the rendered aria-labels and clicking it, but the browser pane reported innerWidth 0 while it was hidden, so state.viewport was zero, isUsableViewport was false and the viewport-width path could not be exercised there. Only a look at Polkadot in a real window can confirm that, and the earlier 1296 to 1264 column reading was taken under that same zero viewport so it does not measure the fix

decision: Make the vacancy search stop on a free spot, matching the invariant its own comment and the API document already stated
why: getInfiniteCanvasVacantRect searched 169 lattice positions around the preferred spot and, when none was clear, returned the candidate with the smallest covered area, which is still an overlap. Three sources already said that was wrong and only the code disagreed. The comment above the candidate list says a full viewport is a reason to look further out and never a reason to stack two windows on one spot. docs/API.md line 396 says the same in the published contract, that a full viewport is not a reason to return an occupied rectangle. So this is a defect against a stated invariant rather than a design choice, and it is the online counterpart of the packing work: placing one new window is the online problem, packing a set is the offline one
evidence: window-placement.ts: the area-summing coveredArea is replaced by an isClear predicate that short-circuits on the first intersection, since every caller only asked whether the area was zero. The least-bad-overlap reduce is deleted. When no candidate is clear the result now sits below unionRects(occupied), reusing the union that geometry.ts already owns. docs/API.md gains the two sentences that make the guarantee explicit, so a caller can place a window without an overlap check of its own
result: VERIFIED BY TRACE, not by the test run, and the distinction matters here. The 817 tests pass unchanged, which proves only that no existing test covered this path, so the green run is not evidence and is not offered as any. The trace is: candidates tile a lattice of step width-plus-gap by height-plus-gap centred on preferred, so an exhausted find means every one of those 169 positions intersects something; the fallback then starts at the bottom edge of the union of everything occupied, and no occupant extends below its own union bound, so that rect intersects nothing by construction and the function always terminates on a clear result. NOT VERIFIED: the visible consequence, which is that a window opened onto a completely full neighbourhood now appears below the crowd rather than stacked on it, and is reachable through the offscreen indicators. Only a look at the running app with a deliberately crowded canvas shows whether that reads better than the overlap did

decision: Frame the result after packing, because a tidier block is a taller one
why: Measuring the feature shipped earlier today found a defect in it. Rows are as wide as the visible region, so packing trades width for height, and past a certain count the block is taller than the screen. Measured on the playground at 24 windows in a 676 by 721 pane, the packed block was 308 by 1708 and only 6 of the 24 windows were still on screen. A user presses the button, sees three rows, and reasonably concludes it did nothing. The framework keeps document operations and view operations separate and every command is one or the other, so packing must not move the camera itself. The consumer composes the two commands instead, which is the same layering the roadmap requires for anything that is not a generic capability
evidence: apps/polkadot/src/hud/canvas-hud.tsx and apps/playground/src/routes/packing.tsx both follow window.pack with view.fitSelection. No framework change, no new affordance: both commands already existed and fitSelection already reads useInfiniteCanvasSelectionBounds, so it frames whatever the pack just selected
result: VERIFIED live at localhost:3300/packing by clicking the real button: visible windows after packing went from 6 of 24 to 24 of 24, with overlapping pairs still zero. Both affected packages check clean. NOT VERIFIED in Polkadot, for the same reason as the row above: the browser pane reports a zero viewport while hidden, so fitSelection cannot be exercised there and only a look in a real window confirms it

decision: Correct backlog E3 and the compositor blueprint: Polkadot projects its relations into the canvas rather than moving them into the connections slice
why: Both documents said Polkadot's connectors become the same connections slice as the workflow-board links. Reading relation-store.ts and connector-geometry.ts before writing the derivation shows they are different concepts, which is the reading the consolidation audit's central finding warns about — parallel structure across genuinely distinct things. A framework connection is keyed by window id, directed, canvas document state, undone by canvas history. A Polkadot relation is keyed by content item id, undirected because findRelation matches either direction, stored in SurrealDB, spans every canvas in the project, and carries its own undo through rememberUndoableAction. The decisive detail is arity: getConnectorRectsByItem returns a list of rects per item because one item can be open in several windows, so one relation draws several connectors, and an edge between two window ids cannot express that
evidence: docs/internal/backlog.md item E3 and the blueprint's engine-first point 2, both corrected in place with the evidence and a pointer between them. apps/polkadot/src/relations/relation-store.ts lines 7 to 165, apps/polkadot/src/canvas/connector-geometry.ts getHiddenConnectorStubs at 151, apps/polkadot/src/content/describe-content.ts getOpenItemIds at 14
result: NOT A CODE CHANGE, and recorded because it stops one. Acting on E3 as written would have moved a durable cross-canvas database fact into per-canvas document state, losing the relation for every canvas that does not hold both windows and collapsing the several-connectors-per-relation case to one. The slice built in a86e6dc is still right for a canvas whose edges are canvas state, which the workflow board's links are; that half of E3 stands unchanged

The framework checks clean across 196 files and the playground across 27; the /drop-tray route renders with its tray, its instruction card and a mounted canvas, and the only console errors carry fixed timestamps from the edit window rather than the current load. NOT VERIFIED, and stated plainly rather than implied: the ghost itself only appears mid-drag, native drag and drop is not reliable to synthesize, and I did not see it draw. decision: Fix the regression 2fadbf6 introduced: framework passes were all forced into the underlay, so the drop preview drew beneath the windows
why: Found while reading the seam for E4, not by a failing check, and it is exactly the defect the previous row flagged as unverified. getFrameworkPasses returned an empty list for anything but the underlay, and the surface then grouped by space rather than by each pass's own placement, so a pass declaring placement overlay was mounted in the underlay anyway. The consumer's version drew in the overlay surface, above the window plane. Moving it to the framework silently pushed it under the windows, which hides the ghost whenever the target is an existing card — and dropping onto a card body is a supported target, so the case that breaks is a real one
evidence: getFrameworkPasses now builds the whole list and filters it by each pass's placement, so a pass states where it paints and is believed. infinite-canvas.tsx mounted the overlay surface only when a consumer supplied overlay sceneLayers, which is never now, so the surface had to learn about framework overlay passes: hasInfiniteCanvasOverlayPass in policy.ts answers that without pulling the GPU stack into the main entry. It also takes hasDropPolicy, because the preview draws from a placement dropPolicy resolves and a canvas taking no drops should not pay for a second GPU surface that can never draw
result: VERIFIED by counting canvases on two live routes, which separates the fix from the cost: /drop-tray, which supplies a dropPolicy, mounts two canvases at z-index 0 and 999999990, so the overlay exists and the preview can paint over the window plane; /workflow-board, which supplies none, mounts one. Both stable across samples. Framework checks clean across 196 files and all three API gates pass. STILL NOT VERIFIED: the ghost drawing during an actual drag, for the same reason as before — native drag and drop is not reliable to synthesize and I have not seen it. What this change establishes is that the surface it needs now exists, which it did not after 2fadbf6

decision: Delete the sceneLayers prop and its placement splitter, closing most of backlog E4
why: Nothing passed sceneLayers any more once the connections and drop-preview passes moved into the framework, so the prop, the two memos that split it by placement, the splitter itself and the plumbing through three components were all carrying a case that no longer exists. The blueprint schedules exactly this: there is no consumer pass list, and a seam kept for a caller that does not exist is the speculative machinery the simple skill bans
evidence: Deleted: InfiniteCanvasDesktopProps.sceneLayers, InfiniteCanvasSceneSurfaceProps.sceneLayers, getSceneLayers in scene-surface.ts, the underlaySceneLayers and overlaySceneLayers memos, the prop on both surface mounts, the default and dependency in CompositorCanvas, and the pass-through from InfiniteCanvasDesktop to the viewport. The overlay mount condition simplifies to hasInfiniteCanvasOverlayPass alone, since the consumer half of it can no longer be non-empty. InfiniteCanvasScenePass stays: it is the framework's own pass shape with 33 internal uses, not a consumer entry point
result: VERIFIED live on three surfaces after the deletion, and the numbers are the same ones the previous commit established, which is the point: /workflow-board still mounts one canvas and still draws its two links, /drop-tray still mounts two because it supplies a dropPolicy, and Polkadot still mounts two with its five windows rendering. Framework, playground and Polkadot all check clean, 817 tests pass, all three API gates are green with the public counts unchanged at 271 and 210. NOT DONE, and the remaining half of E4: sceneSurface is still a prop, so the compositor does not yet mount itself when the /scene entry is present
